## Classical certainty equivalence

In linear--quadratic--Gaussian (LQG) control with output feedback, the optimal action admits a structured representation: solve the **fully observed** stochastic LQG problem to obtain a state-feedback law $\hat π^\star$, form the MMSE state estimate $\hat σ_t(h_t) = \EXP[S_t \mid H_t = h_t]$, and set
$$
  π_t(h_t) = \hat π^\star_t\bigl(\hat σ_t(h_t)\bigr).
$$
This is the classical **certainty equivalence** principle.

Two points are easy to conflate.

1. The comparison model $\ALPHABET M$ is fully observed but still **stochastic**. One does **not** replace process noise by its mean and then solve a deterministic open-loop problem. (That different idea is sometimes also called certainty equivalence in static stochastic optimization; it is not the object of this lecture.)
2. In LQG the construction is **optimal**. Outside LQG, composing a fully observed optimal policy with a state estimate is a **heuristic**. The rest of the lecture makes that heuristic quantitative for finite POMDPs.

## Generalized CE for finite POMDPs

Fix a finite-horizon POMDP with finite spaces $\ALPHABET S$, $\ALPHABET A$, $\ALPHABET Y$, history $H_t = (Y_{1:t}, A_{1:t-1})$, and additive costs $C_t = c_t(S_t, A_t)$. Write $V^π_t(h_t)$ and $V^\star_t(h_t)$ for the history value of a policy $π$ and for the optimal history value, as in lecture 7.

Let $\ALPHABET M$ be the associated **fully observed** MDP
$$
  \ALPHABET M
  =
  \bigl\langle
    \ALPHABET S,\,
    \ALPHABET A,\,
    \{P_t\},\,
    \{c_t\},\,
    T
  \bigr\rangle,
$$
in which the controller sees $S_t$ at time $t$ and $P_t(\cdot \mid s, a)$ is the state transition kernel of the POMDP. Finite $\ALPHABET S$ and $\ALPHABET A$ guarantee an optimal Markov policy $\hat π^\star = (\hat π^\star_1,\dots,\hat π^\star_T)$ with value functions $\{\hat V^\star_t\}$ on $\ALPHABET S$.

Now allow an arbitrary sequence of estimators $\hat σ_t \colon \ALPHABET H_t \to \ALPHABET S$: conditional mean, MAP / mode, last observation, finite window, a learned filter, and so on. Write $\hat S_t = \hat σ_t(H_t)$ for the resulting estimate. The **certainty equivalent** policy generated by $\{\hat σ_t\}$ is
$$
  π^{\mathrm{CE}}_t(h_t)
  =
  \hat π^\star_t\bigl(\hat σ_t(h_t)\bigr).
$$
In words: pretend the estimate is the true state, and play the optimal fully observed action. In the language of lecture 8 this is exactly the lifted AIS policy $π_t = \hat π^\star_t \circ \hat σ_t$.

### Quality of estimation

Equip $\ALPHABET S$ with a metric $d_{\ALPHABET S}$. Define the worst-case conditional estimation error
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ce-eta}
  η_t
  \coloneqq
  \sup_{h_t \in \ALPHABET H_t}
  \EXP\bigl[
    d_{\ALPHABET S}\bigl(S_t, \hat σ_t(h_t)\bigr)
    \bigm| H_t = h_t
  \bigr].
\end{equation}
By the belief lemma of lecture 7 (@lem-belief-policy-independent), the conditional law of $S_t$ given $h_t$ does not depend on the control policy, so $η_t$ is a property of the observation model and the estimator alone.

## Smoothness assumption

Assume the cost and dynamics of $\ALPHABET M$ are Lipschitz in the state: there exist constants $L^c_t, L^P_t \ge 0$ such that for all $s,\tilde s \in \ALPHABET S$ and $a \in \ALPHABET A$,
\begin{align}
  \ABS{c_t(s,a) - c_t(\tilde s,a)}
  &\le
  L^c_t\, d_{\ALPHABET S}(s,\tilde s),
  \label{eq:ce-Lip-c} \\
  W_1\bigl(
    P_t(\cdot \mid s,a),\,
    P_t(\cdot \mid \tilde s,a)
  \bigr)
  &\le
  L^P_t\, d_{\ALPHABET S}(s,\tilde s).
  \label{eq:ce-Lip-P}
\end{align}
As in @thm-value-lipschitz-bound,
$$
  \operatorname{Lip}(\hat V^\star_t)
  \le
  L^c_t + L^P_t\, \operatorname{Lip}(\hat V^\star_{t+1}),
$$
with $\operatorname{Lip}(\hat V^\star_{T+1}) = 0$. Thus Lipschitz constants of $\hat V^\star$ are controlled by $\{L^c_t, L^P_t\}$ alone.

## Main insight: the CE generator is an AIS

The punchline is that certainty equivalence is an AIS policy for a concrete generator whose errors are linear in $η_t$.

:::{#thm-ce-ais}
#### CE as an AIS

Under \eqref{eq:ce-Lip-c}--\eqref{eq:ce-Lip-P}, the compression $\hat σ_t$ with cost approximators $\hat c_t = c_t$ and dynamics approximators $\hat P_t = P_t$ (the primitives of $\ALPHABET M$) is an $\{(ε_t,δ_t)\}$-AIS generator in the sense of @def-ais, with
$$
  ε_t = L^c_t\, η_t,
  \qquad
  δ_t = L^P_t\, η_t + η_{t+1}
$$
(with the convention $η_{T+1} = 0$). Consequently the certainty equivalent policy $π^{\mathrm{CE}}$ coincides with the lifted AIS policy $\hat π^\star \circ \hat σ$, whose approximate MDP is exactly $\ALPHABET M$ and whose approximate optimal value functions are $\{\hat V^\star_t\}$.
:::

Only (AP1) and (AP2) need to be checked. The policy gap is then an instance of @thm-ais-approx-dp (Wasserstein form).

### Verification of (AP1)

:::{#lem-ce-ap1}
#### Cost approximation for CE

For every history $h_t$ and action $a_t$,
$$
  \ABS{
    \EXP\bigl[ c_t(S_t, a_t) \bigm| H_t = h_t,\, A_t = a_t \bigr]
    - c_t\bigl(\hat σ_t(h_t), a_t\bigr)
  }
  \le
  L^c_t\, η_t.
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="false"}
#### Proof

Write $\hat s_t = \hat σ_t(h_t)$. By the triangle inequality and \eqref{eq:ce-Lip-c},
\begin{align*}
  \ABS{
    \EXP\bigl[ c_t(S_t, a_t) \bigm| h_t \bigr]
    - c_t(\hat s_t, a_t)
  }
  &\le
  \EXP\bigl[
    \ABS{c_t(S_t, a_t) - c_t(\hat s_t, a_t)}
    \bigm| h_t
  \bigr]
  \\
  &\le
  L^c_t\,
  \EXP\bigl[
    d_{\ALPHABET S}(S_t, \hat s_t)
    \bigm| h_t
  \bigr]
  \\
  &\le
  L^c_t\, η_t,
\end{align*}
where the last step is \eqref{eq:ce-eta}.
:::

### Verification of (AP2)

:::{#lem-ce-ap2}
#### Dynamics approximation for CE

For every history $h_t$ and action $a_t$, writing
$$
  μ_t(\,\cdot\,)
  =
  \PR\bigl( \hat S_{t+1} \in \cdot \bigm| H_t = h_t,\, A_t = a_t \bigr),
  \quad
  ν_t(\,\cdot\,)
  =
  P_t\bigl(\cdot \bigm| \hat σ_t(h_t), a_t\bigr)
$$
as in @def-ais, we have
$$
  W_1(μ_t, ν_t)
  \le
  L^P_t\, η_t + η_{t+1}.
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="false"}
#### Proof

Write $\hat s_t = \hat σ_t(h_t)$ and let
$$
  \tilde μ_t(\cdot \mid h_t, a_t)
  =
  \PR\bigl( S_{t+1} \in \cdot \bigm| h_t, a_t \bigr)
  =
  \sum_{s \in \ALPHABET S}
  P_t(\cdot \mid s, a_t)\, b_t[h_t](s)
$$
be the predictive law of the true next state. By the triangle inequality for $W_1$,
$$
  W_1(μ_t, ν_t)
  \le
  W_1(μ_t, \tilde μ_t)
  +
  W_1(\tilde μ_t, ν_t).
$$

**Estimate versus true next state.** Coupling $(\hat S_{t+1}, S_{t+1})$ under the joint conditional law given $(h_t, a_t)$ and using the definition of $η_{t+1}$,
\begin{align*}
  W_1(μ_t, \tilde μ_t)
  &\le
  \EXP\bigl[
    d_{\ALPHABET S}\bigl(\hat S_{t+1}, S_{t+1}\bigr)
    \bigm| h_t, a_t
  \bigr]
  \\
  &=
  \EXP\Bigl[
    \EXP\bigl[
      d_{\ALPHABET S}\bigl(\hat σ_{t+1}(H_{t+1}), S_{t+1}\bigr)
      \bigm| H_{t+1}
    \bigr]
    \Bigm| h_t, a_t
  \Bigr]
  \\
  &\le
  η_{t+1}.
\end{align*}

**Dynamics Lipschitz under current error.** Convexity of $W_1$ and \eqref{eq:ce-Lip-P} give
\begin{align*}
  W_1(\tilde μ_t, ν_t)
  &\le
  \sum_{s}
  b_t[h_t](s)\,
  W_1\bigl(
    P_t(\cdot \mid s, a_t),\,
    P_t(\cdot \mid \hat s_t, a_t)
  \bigr)
  \\
  &\le
  L^P_t\,
  \EXP\bigl[
    d_{\ALPHABET S}(S_t, \hat s_t)
    \bigm| h_t
  \bigr]
  \\
  &\le
  L^P_t\, η_t.
\end{align*}
Adding the two estimates yields the claim.
:::

### Invoking the AIS theorem

@thm-ce-ais together with @lem-ce-ap1 and @lem-ce-ap2 feeds @thm-ais-approx-dp with abstract values $\hat V^\star_t$ of $\ALPHABET M$ and $ρ_{\F} = \operatorname{Lip}$ (since $d_{\F} = W_1$).

:::{#thm-ce-gap}
#### Sub-optimality of certainty equivalence

Under \eqref{eq:ce-Lip-c}--\eqref{eq:ce-Lip-P}, the certainty equivalent policy $π^{\mathrm{CE}}$ satisfies
$$
  V^{π^{\mathrm{CE}}}_t(h_t) - V^\star_t(h_t)
  \le
  2 α_t
$$
for every history $h_t$, where
$$
  α_t
  =
  ε_t
  +
  \sum_{τ=t}^{T-1}
  \bigl(
    δ_τ\, \operatorname{Lip}(\hat V^\star_{τ+1})
    + ε_{τ+1}
  \bigr)
$$
and $ε_τ = L^c_τ η_τ$, $δ_τ = L^P_τ η_τ + η_{τ+1}$.
:::

:::{.callout-tip}
#### Reading the bound
Sub-optimality scales with estimation error $\{η_t\}$, amplified by the Lipschitz constants of the fully observed model $\ALPHABET M$. When the filter is accurate ($η_t$ small) and $\ALPHABET M$ is smooth, CE is near-optimal. The only new mathematics relative to lecture 8 is the verification that $(\hat σ, c, P)$ is an AIS generator; the factor $2α_t$ is inherited.
:::

## Example: bounded observation noise

:::{#exm-ce-bounded-noise}
#### Bounded observation noise

Suppose $\ALPHABET Y = \ALPHABET S$ and the observation always lands within radius $r$ of the state:
$$
  d_{\ALPHABET S}(Y_t, S_t) \le r
  \qquad\text{for all realizations.}
$$
Take the estimator to be the last observation, $\hat σ_t(h_t) = y_t$. Then
$$
  \EXP\bigl[
    d_{\ALPHABET S}\bigl(S_t, \hat σ_t(h_t)\bigr)
    \bigm| h_t
  \bigr]
  =
  \EXP\bigl[
    d_{\ALPHABET S}(S_t, y_t)
    \bigm| h_t
  \bigr]
  \le r,
$$
so $η_t \le r$ for every $t$. Under the Lipschitz assumption \eqref{eq:ce-Lip-c}--\eqref{eq:ce-Lip-P},
$$
  ε_t \le r L^c_t,
  \qquad
  δ_t \le r\bigl(1 + L^P_t\bigr).
$$
@thm-ce-gap therefore yields
$$
  V^{π^{\mathrm{CE}}}_t(h_t) - V^\star_t(h_t)
  \le
  2 r\, L^{\ALPHABET M}_t,
$$
where
$$
  L^{\ALPHABET M}_t
  \coloneqq
  L^c_t
  +
  \sum_{τ=t}^{T-1}
  \Bigl(
    \bigl(1 + L^P_τ\bigr)\, \operatorname{Lip}(\hat V^\star_{τ+1})
    + L^c_{τ+1}
  \Bigr)
$$
depends only on the smoothness of $\ALPHABET M$. As $r \to 0$ (vanishing observation noise), the CE policy with $\hat σ_t(h_t) = y_t$ approaches optimality at a linear rate in $r$.
:::

:::{.callout-note}
#### Variant: intermittent degradation
The same proof applies when observations are usually accurate but occasionally degraded. Suppose $d_{\ALPHABET S}(Y_t, S_t) \le r$ on a “good” event and $d_{\ALPHABET S}(Y_t, S_t) \le R$ otherwise, with $\PR(\text{bad} \mid h_t) \le p$ for every history. Then $η_t \le (1-p)r + p R$, and @thm-ce-gap gives the same $2α_t$ bound with this larger $η_t$ in place of $r$. Small noise **or** infrequent degradation both make CE near-optimal.
:::

## When CE is the wrong structure

Certainty equivalence is not appropriate for every POMDP. If the action set includes a costly **sensing** action that reveals the state, a CE policy never chooses to sense: its action is always $\hat π^\star_t(\hat s_t)$ for the fully observed MDP $\ALPHABET M$, which has no reason to pay for information it already treats as free and perfect.

This is exactly the tension in the **when-to-observe** example of lecture 7. There the optimal policy sometimes pays $λ$ to reset the belief to a point mass. A CE rule with $\hat σ_t$ equal to the last observation (or any estimator that ignores the option value of sensing) will not reproduce that tradeoff. The AIS bound remains valid, but $η_t$ need not be small for such an estimator, and a different structured policy (one that occasionally senses) can do better.

## Optional remark: CE with state abstraction

The same argument applies with a state abstraction $φ \colon \ALPHABET S \to \hat{\ALPHABET S}$: estimate $φ(S_t)$, solve the abstract MDP $\widehat{\ALPHABET M}$ from lecture 5, and play $\hat π^\star_t(\hat σ_t(h_t))$. Abstraction error and filter error add inside an effective $η_t$; the AIS theorem again supplies the gap. We do not derive the details here.
